paragraphs.text: It was Christmas Eve, and the city of London was full of holiday cheer. Despite the bitter cold, people were smiling and laughing as they went about their business. Even the horses pulling carts and wagons seemed jollier than usual.

But not everyone was feeling the warm Christmas spirit. A man named Ebenezer Scrooge was still hard at work. The air inside his countinghouse office was nearly as cold as the air outside. Scrooge could afford to keep the building warm if he liked. But he believed in making and saving money, not spending it. He was so miserly that he allowed himself to light only a very small fire. He allowed his employee, Bob Cratchit, an even smaller one.
As the two men worked, the door suddenly flew open. A smiling young man burst in.
"Merry Christmas, Uncle Scrooge!" It was Scrooge's nephew, Fred.
"Bah!" Scrooge said. "Humbug!"
Fred's eyes sparkled with amusement. "Are you calling Christmas a humbug, Uncle? I'm sure you don't mean to say that this wonderful holiday is a bunch of nonsense."
"I certainly do mean that," Scrooge said. "I hate Christmas! And why are you so merry? It's not as if you're wealthy, with nothing to worry about."
"I won't disagree with that," Fred said cheerfully. "I'm not a rich man. But why are you so miserable? Unlike me, you are wealthy. So shouldn't you be cheerful?"
Scrooge rolled his eyes. "I can't believe I live in a world full of fools like you."
"Don't be so cross, Uncle." Fred grinned. "It's Christmas!"
"You can celebrate Christmas in your own way," Scrooge said. "Let me celebrate it in mine."
"Celebrate it?" Fred raised his eyebrows. "But you don't celebrate it."
"Let me ignore it then," Scrooge snapped. "In my opinion celebrating it has never done anyone any good at all."

Fred shrugged. "Christmas has certainly never made me any money. But it is a kind, forgiving, and pleasant time. It's a time when men and women open their hearts and try to help others. Therefore, Uncle, I believe it has done me good. And it will continue to do me good for as long as I live."
Scrooge scowled. "You're a powerful speaker, Fred. You should run for a seat in Parliament."
Fred laughed. "I haven't come to talk about money—or politics. I've come to invite you to dine with us tomorrow on Christmas Day."
"Good afternoon," Scrooge said coldly, clearly dismissing his nephew.
Fred tried once more to convince his uncle to come to dinner.
But Scrooge's voice only got louder. "I said . . . good afternoon!"
Finally Fred shrugged and gave up. "I can see that you're determined to stay angry. Still, I wish you a merry Christmas, Uncle."
"Good afternoon!"
"And a happy New Year," Fred added with a grin.
On his way out, Fred stopped to wish Bob Cratchit a happy holiday. Scrooge's eyes narrowed as he listened to the two men exchanging friendly words.

"Now Cratchit is the one talking about a merry Christmas for no good reason," Scrooge muttered to himself. "What right does that man have to be merry? The fool has chosen to try to support a wife and six children on a tiny salary. It's barely enough for one person, never mind an entire family."
A few minutes later, Fred was gone. But two other people knocked on the door of the office. When Scrooge opened the door, he saw two older gentlemen standing there, smiling and well-dressed.
"This business belongs to Scrooge and Marley, I believe?" one said in a pleasant voice. "Am I speaking to Mr. Scrooge or Mr. Marley?"
"Marley has been dead for seven years," Scrooge said bluntly. He rarely thought about his old partner anymore, even though Jacob Marley had built the business along with him.
"Oh. I'm sorry for your loss, Mr. Scrooge," the second man said with a bow. "We won't take up much of your time. We're only here to ask you to be generous during this festive time of year."
"Yes," the first man added. "We're collecting donations for the poor. Many people lack even basic comforts of life, such as food and warm clothing."
"That's why there are prisons!" Scrooge yelled. "I'd rather support those and let the poor be fed and warmed there. Good afternoon, gentlemen!"
With that, he slammed the door in their startled faces and returned to work.
While Scrooge worked inside his office, the day darkened into night. Outside, the weather grew foggy and damp. The air temperature dropped even lower, making people shiver in their winter coats.
Finally the end of the business day arrived. As soon as Bob Cratchit saw his boss rise from his stool, he leaped to his feet too. He put out his candle and reached for his hat.
Scrooge stared coldly at his employee. "You'll want the whole day off tomorrow for Christmas, I suppose?" he asked in a disagreeable voice.
"Yes." Cratchit smiled uncertainly. "Um, that is, if you don't mind, sir."

"I do mind!" Scrooge said. "And not only that, but I also find it quite unfair. If I held back your pay, people would say you were poorly treated. Meanwhile nobody would consider me poorly treated if I paid you for no work!"
"Christmas comes only once per year, Mr. Scrooge," Cratchit said softly.
Scrooge let out a harrumph. "That's a poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December. But I suppose you may have the day off. Make sure you're early on the following day!"
Cratchit's eyes lit up. "I will be here early, sir! I promise! Thank you!"

The two men shut up the office, and then Cratchit ran off down the street. Scrooge, however, walked slowly, ignoring all signs of the holiday around him. He ate his melancholy dinner in his usual melancholy inn, with only a newspaper for company. Then he walked home toward his apartment, which had once belonged to Jacob Marley.
At the front door of the apartment building, Scrooge put his key in the lock. Then he blinked, startled by something odd.
"Why does the door knocker look so strange?" he thought. "Is it the fog?"
Scrooge leaned in closer for a better look. "M-Marley?" he gasped.

To his shock, the door knocker had taken on the shape of his old partner's face. Marley looked much like himself, with his spectacles resting on his forehead. Yet his face was glowing with an eerie light, and an invisible breeze was stirring his hair.
Suddenly the knocker seemed to freeze, returning to its usual appearance.

Scrooge shook his head and muttered to himself. He was not usually frightened by things looking odd in the dark. Still, he couldn't help feeling uneasy as he unlocked the door and entered the building. He hurried toward the stairs, which were hidden in darkness.

No one else lived in the rundown building. So there was no reason for Scrooge to expect to see anything there. However, tonight he saw something moving on the stairs. Horses were pulling a hearse and galloping up the steps ahead of him!
Scrooge groaned and closed his eyes for a moment. "I must have eaten some bad meat at dinner," he thought. "The inn will hear my complaint tomorrow, Christmas or not!"

He stomped up the stairs and into his apartment. Once again he felt oddly worried. He checked each room to be sure he was alone. To his relief, there was nobody behind the sitting room sofa or under the bed. All the closets looked just as they should.
Finally satisfied, he locked the door behind him. He changed into his slippers and bathrobe, and sat down near the fire with a cup of tea.
Dong! Dong!

He nearly dropped the cup when a bell rang out from behind him. Spinning around, he saw that the bell hanging in the corner was swinging back and forth. Back when the building had been one large house, the bell had been used to summon servants. But since Scrooge had no use for it, he had never heard it ring before.
Suddenly more bells began to ring.
Scrooge felt a terrible dread. "First the door knocker, then the stairs, and now this. What on earth is going on?" he thought.
All at once the bells stopped. Then a loud clanking noise rose from somewhere below. It sounded as if someone was dragging heavy chains across the floor and up the stairs.
"What's that awful sound?" Scrooge whispered.

The clanking sound came closer. Soon it was right outside his door. Then a dark figure slipped into the room. As the fire crackled and flamed higher, Scrooge could finally see his frightening visitor.
"I know you!" Scrooge cried, dropping to the floor in shock. "You're Jacob Marley!"
Scrooge could hardly believe his eyes. His former partner, Jacob Marley, stood there looking like a ghost, metal chains wrapped all around his transparent body.
"What do you want from me, Marley?" Scrooge cried.
"I want many things from you." Marley's voice sounded exactly the same. "In life, I was your partner, Jacob Marley."
"Yes." Scrooge felt his legs wobble. "Can you sit down?"
"I can."
"Let's both do it, then."
The two of them sat near the fire. Scrooge continued to stare at the ghost in disbelief.
Marley cocked his head. "You don't believe in ghosts, Ebenezer, do you?"
"Not normally," Scrooge said. "But tonight, so many strange things—"
"Why do you doubt your senses?" Marley demanded.

"Because little things can affect our senses," Scrooge said. "For example, you could be a hallucination caused by bad food I've eaten, like poorly cooked meat. Whatever you are, you do remind me more of gravy than a grave!"
Scrooge rarely made jokes, for he had little sense of humor. But he was trying to keep down his terror in any way he could. The ghost of Jacob Marley was disturbing him to his bones.
The figure moaned and shook his chains loudly, clearly not amused.
Scrooge held on tightly to his chair to prevent himself from fainting. "Dreadful creature, why are you here?"
"Do you believe in me or not?" Marley demanded.
Scrooge closed his eyes. "I do. You are here so I must believe in you. But why have you come to me?"

"I wear these heavy chains, which I made myself, link by link and yard by yard. They are the result of the poor choices I made while alive." Marley glared at Scrooge with his awful eyes. "You have made the same choices, Ebenezer. You continue to make them."
"Jacob," Scrooge said. "This is terrifying. Say something that will comfort me."
"I have no comfort to give," Marley said. "I am doomed to drag these chains with me as a ghost. It's my punishment for a lifetime of selfishness, pettiness, and greed."
"But you were always so good at business," Scrooge said.

"Business?" Marley scoffed. "Humans should have been my business! Charity, mercy, and kindness should have been my business. But, listen to me closely, Ebenezer. My time with you is short. And I'm here to warn you that you have only one chance of escaping the same fate. Tonight you will be haunted by three ghosts."
Scrooge gulped. "More ghosts? I think I'd rather just go to bed!"
"Without their visits, you are doomed to follow the same path that I walk. These ghosts will show you the way to save yourself. Expect the first one very soon. Good-bye, Ebenezer, and good luck."
Marley backed away, clanking his chains and moaning. Scrooge cowered as the ghost floated out through the window.

After Marley was gone, Scrooge hurried to the window. Outside, the air was filled with phantoms floating here and there, moaning as they went. Every one of them wore chains like Marley's ghost. Scrooge went pale as he recognized some of his old business acquaintances.
Turning away from the dreadful sight, he went to the door to make sure it was locked. Then, holding his head in his hands, he went into his bedroom. He climbed into bed and fell asleep instantly.
Scrooge woke up some time later. It was very dark, and the church bell was ringing. Scrooge counted the bell's chimes, expecting them to stop, as they always did. But they continued on and on.
"How strange," Scrooge thought. "Am I dreaming?"
At last, the chimes stopped, and a loud bong shook the walls. At the same moment, an eerie light filled the room.

Scrooge's eyes opened wide at the sight of a figure standing beside his bed. The figure was a strange combination of a young child and an old man. Its hair was long and white. But its face was smooth, without the slightest wrinkle. It wore a white tunic and held a fresh green holly branch in one hand.
"I suppose you're one of the ghosts that Marley told me about?" Scrooge's voice shook as he spoke.
"I am." The ghost's voice was soft and gentle.
"Do you have a name?" Scrooge asked.
"I am the Ghost of Christmas Past." The spirit clasped Scrooge gently by the arm. "Arise and walk with me."

Scrooge wanted to refuse the ghost's invitation. He had no desire to walk anywhere with such a frightening creature! But it was pointless to resist. The ghost's grasp was as gentle as a child's hand, but it was stronger than the grip of any adult.
The ghost pulled Scrooge toward one of the windows.
"Wait, spirit!" Scrooge cried. "I'm a mortal, not a ghost, remember? And we're on the second floor. If I fall out the window, I'll get hurt!"
"Don't worry," the ghost said. He touched Scrooge on his heart. "My touch on your heart is all it takes to keep you safe."

With that, both spirit and Scrooge passed through the wall. Instead of emerging onto the street in front of the apartment building, they stood on an open road. The city and night had vanished. It was now a cold winter day in the country. Snowy fields lay on either side of the road, and the air felt clear and crisp.
"Good heavens!" Scrooge cried, clasping his hands as he looked around. "I know exactly where we are. I grew up in this place!"
The Ghost of Christmas Past touched Scrooge's heart again.

Scrooge gasped as various pleasant odors floated past his nose. Each one reminded him of the few happy moments from his childhood. There was the scent of his mother's lavender perfume. Then came the buttery aroma of the cookies his nanny had baked for him. Next he smelled the sweetness of his beloved sister's favorite candy.
"Your lip is trembling," the ghost said in its mild voice. "And what is that upon your cheek?"
Scrooge touched his cheek, which felt moist with tears. "Never mind," he said with a catch in his voice. "Lead me where you wish."
"Don't you remember the way?" the spirit asked.

"I do remember," Scrooge said. His feet carried him quickly along the road to a town. Scrooge recognized the bridge over the river, the church steeple, and everything else he saw. They passed a pair of shaggy ponies trotting along with laughing boys on their backs. Scrooge recognized the boys as well, though by now, they should be old men like him. He called out to them, but they didn't respond.
"These people are shadows of things that have been," the ghost said. "They can't see or hear us."
"I see," Scrooge said, watching more happy people go by.
"Merry Christmas!" An older man tipped his hat to several young ladies.
"And a merry Christmas to you, sir!" the ladies said with good cheer.
Finally Scrooge reached a house that was even more familiar than the rest. In front of it, a young boy was building a snowman.
Scrooge's eyes widened. "Why, that . . . that boy is me!"

The young Ebenezer finished the snowman by placing a hat on its head. Then he grinned and ran into the house. A moment later he reappeared, pulling a laughing young woman by the hand. She was holding a baby wrapped in a blanket.
"Oh," Scrooge whispered. "It's my mother—she's alive again. My beautiful, kind mother, and my dear little sister too."
"Look, Mother!" Young Ebenezer was grinning proudly. "I built a snowman for baby Fan!"
"It's wonderful, my clever son," Mother said. She held up the baby so tiny Fan could see too. The baby cooed and waved her plump arms.
Suddenly a large man burst out of the house, scowling at the scene. "What's going on out here? It's far too cold to be outdoors without proper clothes!"
"It's all right, darling," Mother said quickly. "I came out for only a moment. Ebenezer wanted to show his snowman to Fan and me. That's all."

"Humbug!" the man snapped. "Ebenezer should be indoors, reading. What sort of businessman will he become while wasting time on silly activities like building snowmen? And is that my best hat?" His face turned red with outrage. Then he stomped over and grabbed the hat off the snowman, accidentally knocking off its head. "Get inside, all of you. If the baby gets sick, I'll blame you, boy!"
Scrooge shuddered along with his younger self.
"I remember that day," he said as he watched young Ebenezer slink back into the house behind his parents. "A short time later, my father sent me off to boarding school."
The ghost nodded. "Come with me. We have much more to see."
After one last glance at the sad, headless snowman, Scrooge obeyed.

The ghost beckoned for Scrooge to continue through the town and walk along a narrow lane. After a while they approached a large, red-brick building with a belltower. Scrooge felt a chill when he saw it. The building had once been a fine mansion. But it had fallen on hard times since then, with mossy walls and broken windows.

"I see that you remember your old boarding school," the ghost said. "It's nearly Christmas Day, but it's not quite deserted. There's still one child there, a solitary boy neglected by his friends and family."
"I know." Scrooge choked back a sob. He knew exactly which boy had been left alone at school. He wanted to turn away from the building, but the spirit pulled him inside.

They entered a room at the back of the school. Inside, Scrooge saw himself as a boy, sitting at a desk. The boy was just a year or two older than the one who had built the snowman. He was all alone with only his books for company.
Tears streamed down Scrooge's face as he remembered the day.
"My father wouldn't allow me to come home for the Christmas holiday," he whispered. "He said it would do me more good to stay here and study. He said nobody at home would miss me."
"Now let's see another Christmas," the ghost said gently.
The young Ebenezer at the desk grew taller, turning into a young man. The school remained empty because once more, all the other students had gone home for Christmas.
Young Ebenezer started pacing back and forth, occasionally glancing out the window. His face wore a look of despair and gloom.
Then there was a noise outside the door. Young Ebenezer spun around to face it. The door flew open, and a girl with shiny curls and a happy face burst in.
Scrooge recognized her at once.
"It's my younger sister," he said with wonder. "My beloved little Fan. She looks just as I remember her."
"Ebenezer!" The little girl flung herself at the young man. He caught her in a hug. "I have come to bring you home, my dear, dear brother!"
Young Ebenezer gasped. "What? Home?"

"Yes, home!" Fan said, laughing. "Home for good, forever and ever. Father is so much kinder than he used to be. He spoke so gently to me one day, I got the courage to ask him again to bring you home."
"And he said yes?" Young Ebenezer sounded shocked.

"Yes! He sent me in the coach to fetch you. And he said that since you're nearly a man now, there's no need to return to school ever again." Fan beamed. "We'll all be together for Christmas, and we'll have the merriest time in the world!"
"Oh, Fan, I can't believe it," young Ebenezer said. "How wonderful."
The ghost turned to Scrooge. "Your sister was always a delicate creature. A breath might have knocked her over. But she had a big heart."
"So she did." Scrooge nodded. "I won't argue with you about that."
"She lived long enough to have her own children, did she not?" the ghost asked.
"One son," Scrooge said uneasily. He couldn't help thinking of Fred's visit earlier in the day—and how harshly he'd dismissed his nephew.

The ghost touched Scrooge's heart, and now they stood in a busy section of London. It was Christmas Eve again, and the streetlights cast a warm glow over the cold scene. The ghost stopped in front of a warehouse.
"I know where we are!" Scrooge said. "I was an apprentice here as a young man."
He followed the ghost inside. An old gentleman in a wig sat at a very tall desk in the center of the room. Scrooge nearly laughed with delight as he gazed at the man.
"Why, it's old Fezziwig! Bless his heart, it's Fezziwig alive again!"
At that moment Mr. Fezziwig looked at the clock and laid down his pen. "Yo, ho, Ebenezer! Dick!" he called.
Scrooge saw himself as a young man come hurrying into the room. He was followed by another young man, someone Scrooge hadn't seen in years.
"That's Dick Wilkins," Scrooge said. "He was once quite impressed with me, as I recall."
"No more work tonight, my boys," Fezziwig said, grinning at the two young men. "It's Christmas Eve. Let's clear space for our holiday party!"

Young Ebenezer and Dick Wilkins didn't need to be told twice by old Fezziwig. Quick as a wink, the young men cleared away the desks and other furniture in the warehouse. Soon the large room looked as open and inviting as a ballroom.

In came a fiddler who began playing a joyous holiday tune. Mrs. Fezziwig arrived next, all smiles, followed by her daughters. There was dancing and music and laughter and good cheer. Several guests approached Fezziwig to thank him.

As he watched the scene before him, Scrooge seemed to become a different person. Unaware of what he was doing, he hummed along with the music, watched the dancers, and sniffed the food. He nearly forgot about the spirit standing beside him.

But then the ghost pointed to the guests lined up to talk to Fezziwig. "It looks like your former boss didn't have to do much to earn the gratitude of these folks. He spent only a small amount of money to put on this Christmas party. Tell me, is that enough for him to deserve such praise and gratefulness from his guests?"

"Yes!" Scrooge blurted out, suddenly remembering how much he had admired Fezziwig. "He was our boss, and he could make us happy or unhappy. It doesn't matter how much he spent on the party. The happiness he gave us was so great—it's as if it cost him a fortune. I . . ." Scrooge's words trailed off and he went silent.
"What's the matter?" the ghost asked.
"Nothing," Scrooge said, looking down. "I just wish I could say a word or two to my own employee right now, that's all."
The ghost reached toward Scrooge again. "My time with you is growing short. We must move on now."
After another touch from the ghost, Scrooge found himself in a shabby bedroom that he'd never seen before. A woman sat up in bed, looking tired. She was holding a tiny baby bundled in a blanket.
"Where are we, spirit?" Scrooge asked, feeling confused. "I thought you were showing me things from my own past. I've never been to this place before, and I don't know that woman."
The ghost pointed to the door just as it opened, and a man came in. It was Bob Cratchit, Scrooge's clerk, looking several years younger than he was.
"Here's your water, my love," Cratchit said, handing a cup to the woman with the baby.
"Thank you." She accepted it with a smile and had a long drink. "Would you like to hold our new son, Bob?"
"Do you think it's all right?" Cratchit looked eager but also nervous. "He's so much smaller than our others were when they were born! I don't want to hurt him."
"You won't." Cratchit's wife held up the bundle, beaming with joy.
Cratchit moved closer to take the baby from his wife. As Cratchit gently rocked him, the baby's large eyes gazed up at him.
"You're so beautiful," Cratchit whispered to the baby. "My perfect boy, my beloved little Tiny Tim."
"Tiny Tim?" Scrooge shook his head. "I believe he's the youngest of the children whom Cratchit feeds on his small salary. But, spirit, what does this family scene have to do with me?"
Instead of providing an answer, the spirit asked a question. "Who decides the amount of your clerk's salary?"
"Well, I do, of course!" Scrooge snapped. "I pay him what his work is worth to me. No more, no less."
The ghost tilted its head in reply.
Scrooge frowned, reading disapproval in the ghost's expression. He glanced back at Bob Cratchit, who was still cooing over his newborn son.

"I am a good man of business," Scrooge muttered. "You may ask anyone, spirit, and they'll tell you the same thing. Besides, if I paid my employee more than his worth, everyone would call me a sentimental fool. I would never receive fair treatment in business again. Instead my associates would try to cheat me and take advantage of my weakness."

The Ghost of Christmas Past didn't say anything. Instead it touched Scrooge's heart again, transporting both of them into a modest sitting room. A man and a woman were sitting in front of a crackling fire.
Scrooge went pale, instantly recognizing the woman. "No, spirit! I beg you with all my heart, do not show me this part of my past!"

The man sitting in front of the fire was once more a younger version of Scrooge. However, the man had aged since the party at Fezziwig's. His face no longer looked shy and eager. Now there was a hardness in his eyes and around his mouth.
The young woman beside him had tears in her eyes. Scrooge felt his heart twist with pain as he looked at lovely Belle. He had been in love with her long ago.
"A new idol has displaced me in your heart," Belle said. "I hope it can cheer and comfort you in the future, as I would have tried to do."
Ebenezer looked confused. "I don't understand. What idol has displaced you?"
"Money," Belle said sadly.
Ebenezer scoffed. "That's the way of the world, Belle. Soft-hearted people might say it's wrong to think about money, but nobody wants to be poor, do they?"
"No, but it's possible to fear poverty too much," she said. "You've set aside all your other hopes and dreams. Now your only passion is making money, more and more money."
Ebenezer shrugged. "That's because I'm wiser than most people in this world. And you're wrong to say that money is my only passion. My love for you hasn't changed at all."

She shook her head. "When we first met, we were both poor but content. But you have changed, Ebenezer, which means your feelings toward me have changed too. Back when we met, you were a completely different man."
"I was a boy," he said impatiently. "I didn't understand wealth back then."
"It's something much more than that," Belle said. "That's why I've reached another sad conclusion."
"What is it?" Ebenezer said.
A tear slipped down Belle's cheek. "You once promised to marry me and take care of me. But I must release you from your promise."
"What?" Ebenezer looked startled. "I don't want you to release me from my promise. So why are you doing this?"
Belle sighed. "Because you aren't the same man who made that promise. Imagine if we were to meet for the first time today. Would you bother trying to win my heart?"
Ebenezer hesitated. "Of course I would! You think I wouldn't?"

"I wish I believed you would still try to win my heart. But I believe you would never choose a poor girl today. You'd never choose a girl with no family money to bring to a marriage. Not when you value everything in the world by how much it costs."
"Belle, I . . ."
Belle took a deep breath. "Therefore, with a full heart, I release you. May you be happy in the life you have chosen."
Ebenezer opened his mouth again and looked ready to protest. But at the sight of Belle's determined face, he merely nodded and left.
Scrooge watched Belle collapse in tears.
"Spirit, show me no more!" he cried. "Why do you delight in torturing me? Please take me home!"
The ghost stretched out its finger. "We must see one more shadow."

Scrooge found himself in a different room. A beautiful young woman sat near the fire, and for a moment, he thought she was Belle. Then he spied a middle-aged woman nearby. That was Belle, and he guessed that the younger woman was her daughter.

The room was in an uproar, with several children racing around shouting and laughing. Scrooge was so agitated by seeing Belle again that he didn't bother trying to count her children. Instead he watched as Belle and her oldest daughter laughed at the younger ones' noisy antics.

Suddenly the door flew open, and a smiling man entered, his arms loaded with holiday gifts. The children raced over, nearly smothering him with hugs while shouting joyful greetings. The man finally managed to make his way past them to Belle. Leaning down, he gave her a fond kiss.
Scrooge couldn't help imagining himself in the other man's place.
"What if I had married Belle, as we'd planned long ago?" he thought. "What if I were the one coming home to a house full of children who were happy to see me?"
Scrooge closed his eyes. "Stop!" he cried, trying to banish such thoughts from his mind. "Spirit, I don't want to see any more of this scene!"
But the ghost sounded unmoved by Scrooge's pain. "You must see more. And you will see it."
Slowly Scrooge opened his eyes. Belle and her husband were now sitting together by the fireplace. The children were quieter now, playing with their new toys.
"Belle," her husband said, turning toward her with a smile. "I saw an old friend of yours this afternoon."
"Who was it?" she asked.
"Guess!" he said.
"I have no idea!" she said with a laugh. Then her eyes widened. "I know who it was! Mr. Scrooge!"

"Mr. Scrooge it was," Her husband grinned. "I passed by the window of his office earlier this evening. Unlike all the other offices on the street, his building wasn't shuttered for the holiday. And, of course, there was a candle burning inside." His smile faded, and he shook his head sadly. "I hear his partner, Jacob Marley, lies near death. And yet Mr. Scrooge sat there at work, just as he did when his sister was dying several years ago. Soon he'll be quite alone in the world, won't he? By now, Mr. Marley must be the only person who willingly spends time with him."
"I suppose so," Belle said softly. "I do pity him, even after all the pain he caused me long ago."
"Spirit!" Scrooge cried. "I can't bear watching Belle. Take me home and haunt me no more."
Scrooge turned, lunging toward the ghost. But just before he reached it, he fell to the floor in a deep sleep.

When Scrooge awoke, he was back in his own bed. He sat up and looked around nervously. "Come, spirit number two, if you're still planning a visit," he said in a shaky voice. "I just want to get this strange business over with."
But nothing came. A quarter of an hour passed. Scrooge got up and paced anxiously around his room.
Finally he noticed a red glow coming from beneath his bedroom door.
"That's no normal firelight," Scrooge thought. He put his hand on the doorknob.
A strange, deep voice called out, "Ebenezer Scrooge! Please enter."

Scrooge trembled but obeyed. He stepped into his sitting room, though it didn't look much like his sitting room anymore. The walls and ceiling were hung with so many branches and vines that it looked like a forest grove. A mighty blaze was burning in the fireplace, far larger and hotter than any fire that Scrooge had ever built.

When Scrooge stepped forward, his slipper hit something on the floor. Glancing down, he was surprised to see items from a feast. There were roasted turkeys and geese and wreaths of sausages. There were plum puddings and barrels of oysters. He saw red apples as well as enormous bowls of punch.
Right in the middle of all that food sat a jolly giant, grinning as he held a glowing torch.
"Come in!" the spirit said. "I am the Ghost of Christmas Present. Look at me!"

His voice was friendly, and so was his expression. He wore a simple green robe bordered with white fur, and his feet were bare. Upon his mass of dark brown curls sat a holly wreath decorated with icicles.
"Spirit," Scrooge said humbly, "take me wherever you like. I have already learned some lessons tonight, and I'm ready for more."
The spirit chuckled. "Touch my robe."
Scrooge did as he was told, grabbing onto the edge of the garment. Suddenly all the food and greenery disappeared. So did the room, the fire, and the night.
They were standing on a city street on Christmas morning. It had snowed heavily, and everywhere Scrooge looked, people were out shoveling their stoops and rooftops.

"It must be bitterly cold out," Scrooge said. Even though he couldn't feel the weather, he could see the shovelers' red noses and cheeks. The wind was blowing drifts of snow around, and icicles dripped from every surface.
"Yes, it's very cold," the ghost said.
"But these people all seem so cheerful," Scrooge said. "Just look at them."
He watched as a young man tossed a snowball from one rooftop toward another rooftop. It hit another young man, who shouted with glee and threw one back.
Several women were sweeping a stoop nearby. One started humming a festive tune. Soon all of them were singing a carol while they worked.
Scrooge shook his head in wonder at the people's joy. "Why are they so happy?" he thought. "I don't understand any of this."
But before he could ask the spirit about it, the ghost swept him away to another place.

Scrooge quickly realized that he hadn't traveled very far this time. He was standing with the Ghost of Christmas Present in a different part of London. A church bell was striking the time—one in the afternoon.

Again, as Scrooge looked around, he saw people enjoying the day. There was a man roasting chestnuts over an open fire, and people hanging garlands of holly and mistletoe. Carolers sang while others hummed along.
"Why aren't any of these people working?" Scrooge muttered. "They're all wasting their time!"
The ghost had stopped in front of a small meat shop. Scrooge joined him and peered in the window.
"That's quite a turkey," Scrooge said, eyeing an enormous bird hanging from a hook. "It would take a great number of people to eat it. I wonder how much it costs."
"Papa, look at that huge turkey!" a high-pitched voice cried out before the ghost could respond.

Scrooge spun around and saw a familiar face. "Why, it's Bob Cratchit," he said in surprise. He squinted at the frail child sitting on his clerk's shoulder. The boy was waving a crutch and smiling from ear to ear.
"And I suppose that's Tiny Tim," Scrooge said, thinking of the weak little baby he'd seen earlier.
"It's a huge turkey indeed, my boy," Cratchit said. "What sort of king or emperor do you suppose might buy it?"

Tiny Tim giggled. "I know! The queen is going to order it for the palace! And maybe she'll invite our whole family to dine with her. I bet we'll eat oyster soup and buttered potatoes and a plum pudding as big as me!"

Cratchit chuckled, though his eyes looked rather sad. "That sounds wonderful, Tim. But how would you know which fork to use for each course?" He winked. "One must know such things to dine with the queen at the palace, you see."
Tiny Tim giggled again. "I would just watch Her Majesty, and use the same forks that she uses."

"Clever boy!" Cratchit said. He gently squeezed Tiny Tim's legs and smiled. "That sounds like a fine plan. But just in case our royal invitation doesn't arrive, your mother is planning a feast for us to enjoy later."
"That sounds even better, Papa," Tiny Tim said. "I bet Mama is a much better cook than the queen. Now let's go watch the ice skaters in the park. Can we, please?"
"Of course we can." Turning away from the shop window, Cratchit started toward the park.

Scrooge followed with the spirit, amazed that his clerk was spending the whole day carrying his child around the city. Cratchit and Tiny Tim took their time in reaching the park. Along the way they stopped to admire the holiday decorations on houses and lampposts. They exclaimed over the beautiful things in the shop windows. They talked and laughed together about all of it.

Scrooge shook his head. "They're having so much fun together," he thought. He couldn't understand their bright cheer when there was so much for the Cratchit family to worry about. They were not only poor but also had to concern themselves with the small boy's health.
Finally Cratchit and Tiny Tim reached the park. The lake was frozen solid, and skaters were gliding over the frozen surface on ice skates.
Tiny Tim watched the skaters for a while with a serious expression. "Ice skating looks like fun, Papa," he said. "Do you think I'll ever be strong enough to do it?"
"I'm absolutely sure you will skate one day, son." Cratchit smiled, though once again, Scrooge detected a flicker of pain in his clerk's expression. "Now, Tim, shall we go and finish our errands?"

This time the spirit made no move to follow Cratchit and Tiny Tim. So, Scrooge stayed in place too. He watched Cratchit wind his way through the park. Scrooge was unable to stop thinking about what he'd heard Cratchit say to Tiny Tim.
"Cratchit is a fool if he thinks his son will ever be able to skate," Scrooge snapped. "The boy can't even walk without using his crutch! Why would Cratchit tell him such a thing? It's a lie!"
"Perhaps Cratchit thinks it will make Tiny Tim happy to imagine skating," the ghost said quietly. "Now, come, for we have more errands to do ourselves."
The ghost waved his arm, and the skaters and the park disappeared.
"Ha-ha!"
At first Scrooge saw only blackness, but then the sound of a man's laughter rang out.
"That laugh sounds familiar," Scrooge thought.

Soon his vision cleared, and he saw that he was in a bright room filled with people. His nephew, Fred, was holding his belly, laughing heartily. His laughter was contagious, and soon his wife started laughing too. So did the other people gathered in the room, adults and children alike.
"He said that Christmas was a humbug and dismissed me," Fred said. "Can you believe it?"
"That's what I said earlier!" Scrooge realized. Was Fred talking about him?
"I can believe he'd say those things," his wife said, her laughter fading. "That man can't see the good in anything."
Scrooge was startled to hear Fred's wife insult him that way, as she was generally a kind and polite woman.
"He's a comical old fellow, that's the truth," Fred said. "He's not as pleasant or as kind as he could be, that's for sure. However, I try not to judge others."
His wife's sister rolled her eyes. "I'll judge Ebenezer Scrooge for you then. His only good quality is his wealth!"

Fred shrugged. "My uncle's wealth is of no use to him. He doesn't do any good with it. He doesn't even make himself comfortable with it. He lives in that small, dreary apartment and hoards his money, which can't possibly make him happy."
"I have no patience with him," his wife said.
Her sister and several others nodded their agreement.

Fred smiled at them. "I feel sorry for him, which means I can't stay very angry with him. I mean, who suffers from his bad temper? He does! For example, he has decided to dislike us, so he won't come and dine with us, even on Christmas. What's the consequence? He misses out on a good dinner and some pleasant moments that he might actually enjoy."
"Your uncle's company might do us harm," a young man called out, which made several other guests laugh again.
"I give my poor old uncle the same invitation every year," Fred said, "whether he likes it or not. I certainly don't make his mood any worse by showing up at his office."
His wife nodded. "That's true. His mood is always foul! It's a shame that your kindness, though, doesn't inspire him to help his poor clerk somehow."
"Speaking of Bob Cratchit, I saw him earlier today," Fred said. "He was carrying that little son of his, the one they call Tiny Tim."
"Oh, that poor boy," a woman said. "He's been sickly since the day he was born. But he's such a sweet child!"

"Indeed he is." Fred shook his head. "Today Tiny Tim couldn't stop talking about seeing the ice skaters in the park. And he told me all about a big turkey in one of the shops." Fred smiled briefly before his expression went serious again. "Tiny Tim didn't look well. I fear the boy doesn't have long to live."

His wife turned to gaze at their own children, who were playing at the other end of the room. "Oh no," she said softly. She brushed away a few tears before turning back to the others. "Fred, we've turned things far too solemn for Christmas. Let's have some fun."
Scrooge watched as the group played music and sang songs together. After that, everyone played games, with the children joining in.
Scrooge had always been impatient with games, which he considered a waste of time. But tonight he couldn't stop himself from smiling as Fred and his guests enjoyed themselves.

One of the games was called Yes and No. Fred announced that he was thinking of something, and that the others had to figure out what it was. However, he could only answer their questions with a simple "yes" or "no."
"Are you thinking of a beast?" a tall woman called out.
"Yes!" Fred replied.
"Is it something we might serve for dinner?"
"No!"
"Is it a savage animal?"
"Yes!"
"Does it grunt?"
"Yes!"
"Is it scary?" a child asked with a shiver.
"Yes!"
"I know who it is!" Fred's sister-in-law clapped her hands and grinned. "I know exactly the beast you're thinking of, Fred! It's your uncle Scrooge!"
Everyone at the party, including Fred, burst into loud laughter. But Scrooge frowned. Fred's sister-in-law had just called him a scary beast!
The guests at Fred's party were still laughing at the idea of Ebenezer Scrooge as a scary beast.
At last Fred stopped laughing and managed to speak again.
"You're wrong, my dear sister-in-law," Fred said. "I was thinking of a bear , not my uncle Scrooge."
"Well, your uncle fits just as well," Mary said. "Indeed, I can't imagine a more savage, growling, frightening beast than Mr. Scrooge!"
Scrooge turned to the spirit. "I hope it's time to leave this dreadful scene."
The spirit nodded and then whisked him away again.

This time they arrived in a much larger, finer house than Fred's home. A Christmas party was going on here too. However, this celebration was taking place in a grand ballroom with two musicians. The gentlemen were dressed in their finest suits, and all the women wore lovely, formal dresses.
"Oh, I know that fellow there," Scrooge said, recognizing a business acquaintance among the crowd. "Oh! And that tall gentleman over there too."
Looking around more closely, he realized he knew many of the men gathered in the ballroom. They were all of the most successful businessmen in London, in fact.
"But what is this place, spirit?" Scrooge asked. "Why are all these people gathered here together?"
The spirit drifted closer to one small group of men. Scrooge followed the spirit and listened to the men's conversation.
"I congratulate you on hosting another splendid holiday celebration, Cavendish," a man said. He lifted his glass to Mr. Cavendish.
"Yes, all of London's most important businessmen are here!" another man added. "And we're having a wonderful time."
A third man chuckled. " Nearly everyone is here, you mean. I don't see old Ebenezer Scrooge enjoying himself on the dance floor. Did you, er, forget to invite him again, Cavendish?"

"Oh, what a shame." Cavendish smirked and tapped his own head playfully. "I can't imagine how the most important guest slipped my mind. After all, the old boy is the life of the party everywhere he goes, isn't he?"
At that, the businessmen all laughed loudly.
Scrooge scowled. "How dare they speak of me this way!" he said. "I've never done anything to harm them. And yet here they are mocking and degrading me without mercy!"

The spirit was silent for a moment. "It's true that you've done nothing to harm them," he finally said. "Yet, you've done nothing to help them either." He gestured at one of the men. "When Mr. Aston lost his wife last year, did you attend the funeral? When Mr. Cavendish needed a loan for his newest business, did you step up and offer to help him?"
"Of course not!" Scrooge snapped. "Those things had nothing to do with me. However, my business is successful too. These men could include me in their gatherings."

"If you say so." The spirit shrugged. "However, you might say that their parties and celebrations have nothing to do with you either. If you can't spare a thought for their troubles, why do you expect them to spare any thoughts of you? Or invite you to their social events?"
Scrooge grunted. He couldn't argue with the spirit's logic. And before this strange night, he wouldn't have cared one bit about attending this party.

"I'm not that earnest young man dancing with his friends at Fezziwig's," Scrooge said to the spirit. "Not anymore. I have more important things to occupy my thoughts." Just then something flashed in his mind. "Although, I must admit, sometimes I do think of that silly fellow Dick Wilkins from Fezziwig's business. I wonder what became of him."
The spirit snapped his fingers. The grand ballroom disappeared, replaced by a modest tailor's shop.
Scrooge watched as the tailor bent over a garment. He seemed to be mending a jacket while its owner, a young man, waited.

"Thank you so much for opening your shop on Christmas," the young man said. "It's so very kind of you. I was afraid to show up for Christmas dinner at my father-in-law's house with a rip in my coat. My wife would faint from embarrassment!"
"I'm happy to do it, Mr. Perry. After all, my own wife would be horrified if I turned away someone in need at Christmastime." The tailor looked up and smiled around a mouthful of pins.
That was when Scrooge recognized him.
"Why, that's him, spirit!" Scrooge said. "It's Dick Wilkins!"

"I don't understand why he's a tailor," Scrooge said, watching Dick Wilkins return to his stitching. "Wilkins was no great business genius. But he worked hard and he had me as an example. He could have had a career in business and made a lot more money."
"I suppose so," the Ghost of Christmas Present said. "We must go. My time grows short, and we have more to see."
Abruptly Scrooge found himself standing in front of an unfamiliar house. It was a humble place, smaller and shabbier even than Fred's.
"Where are we?" Scrooge asked. "I don't recognize this place at all."
"You will recognize the people who live here," the spirit replied.

They drifted in through the wall. Inside was a woman wearing a dress that had been patched many times. She'd decorated it with new ribbons, probably to make it look more festive. Her daughter named Belinda was helping her mash potatoes in a rough wooden bowl. Nearby, a boy called Peter was laying out battered plates and forks on the table.
"Who are these people?" Scrooge asked. "You said I would know them."
Suddenly the door flew open. A young boy and girl raced in with snow in their hair.
"You're back, Sam and Sarah!" Peter said.
"The church bells are ringing!" Sam cried.
"Yes, Father and Tiny Tim will be home soon," Sarah said.

"Tiny Tim?" Scrooge said. "Oh! This must be Bob Cratchit's house." He looked at his companion for confirmation, but none was provided. The spirit was watching a young woman hurry in after the children. She was hardly out of her teens, with rosy cheeks.
"Merry Christmas, Mother," she called happily.
The woman dropped her fork and rushed to embrace her daughter. "Martha, my dear! I'm so happy you could come."
"I wouldn't want to be anywhere else for Christmas." Martha hugged her tightly. Then she hugged Belinda and Peter. "You've both grown so tall!"
Sam peeked out the front window. "Here come Father and Tiny Tim. Quick, Martha—hide! You can surprise them!"
"Hide, Martha, hide!" Sarah said excitedly.

The two younger children hurried Martha behind the coat rack while Peter and Belinda looked on with amusement. A moment later the door opened again to reveal Bob Cratchit. Tiny Tim was perched upon his shoulder, clutching his little wooden crutch as usual.
"Merry Christmas, family!" Cratchit looked around. "Oh dear, where's our Martha? I thought she'd be here by now."
Sam stifled a giggle.
But then Martha stepped into view. "I can't stand to tease you, Father. Here I am!"
Her father swung Tiny Tim to the ground, holding him steady while the boy got his crutch in place. Then he hugged Martha tightly.
"We're all here together," he said with a wide smile. "Now it feels like Christmas!"
"The goose is almost ready, Tiny Tim," Belinda said. "Come and see!"
Tim hobbled off after her, using his crutch to help himself along.
Mrs. Cratchit watched him go. "And how was our little Tim?" she asked her husband quietly.
"As good as gold," Cratchit said. "He never seems to mind that he can't do all of the things that other children do. He's happy watching the skaters, though he did ask about skating one day."

Mrs. Cratchit took her husband's hand. "I'm happy just to have him still with us." Her voice was nearly a whisper. Then she cleared her throat and spoke loudly so that the children could hear her. "Now that your father's home, let's eat before the food gets cold!"

The whole family sat down to enjoy the meal. Scrooge couldn't help observing that it was much more modest than the meals he'd seen elsewhere. The goose was so small, it looked more like a duck. There was hardly enough applesauce and mashed potatoes to go around. But the family didn't seem to notice.
"There was never a better goose than this one!" Bob said. "I've never tasted anything so flavorful."
"Me neither," Peter said, helping himself to another piece.
"And the potatoes are the best you've ever made, Mother!" Belinda said.
Mrs. Cratchit beamed. "I was afraid I might have used too much salt."
"Not at all," Martha said. "Everything is perfect."
Bob smiled. "A Merry Christmas to us all, my dears."
"Merry Christmas!" the family said together.
Tiny Tim chimed in too. "God bless us, everyone."
Bob Cratchit reached for Tiny Tim's hand. He squeezed it, looking at the frail little boy with deep love in his eyes.
"Cratchit adores that child," Scrooge said. "Spirit . . ." He paused to look at the ghost. "You must tell me, will Tiny Tim live to see another Christmas?"

"I'm afraid I see a vacant seat at next year's table," the spirit said solemnly. "I see a tiny crutch leaning against the empty chair." He turned to look at Scrooge. "If nothing happens to change the course of the future, the child will die before another Christmas arrives."

"No, no." Scrooge found himself filled with sadness at this terrible news. He looked again at Tiny Tim's little hand, still clasped in his father's loving grip. "Oh no, kind spirit. Please tell me the boy will be spared!"

"I'm surprised to hear such a request from you," the spirit said. "Your only concern with this child before tonight was how much it must cost to support him. You even hoped that his father didn't use him as an excuse to ask you for a raise."
Scrooge's face twisted with guilt. "I didn't mean it," he muttered. "I was just . . ."
At that moment he heard his own name. Bob Cratchit had raised a glass for a toast.
"To Mr. Scrooge, the provider of this feast!"
His wife scowled. "The provider of this feast? I won't drink to the health of a cold, stingy man like Mr. Scrooge."
"My dear," Bob Cratchit said mildly, "it's Christmas."
"Then I'll drink to his health for your sake and for the season," she said. "Not for Mr. Scrooge, who's the ogre of this family. He pays you as little as he can get away with."
"Merry Christmas and Happy New Year to Mr. Scrooge," Tiny Tim said. "Everyone deserves a blessing at Christmastime!"
Even his mother couldn't disagree with that, and so the family drank the toast.

"I'm grateful they're thinking of me," Scrooge muttered. "But blessings and toasts have little value in the real world. Cratchit should spend more time on figuring out how to help his sick child. It's a desperate situation."

Suddenly the house and the family disappeared. Scrooge stood once more on a city street. It was dark, and snow was falling, but the warm glow of fires lightened the gloom around them. Scrooge and the spirit began walking along, peeking through one window after another. They saw a family preparing for a cozy dinner with plates warming over the fire. A plump, smiling woman closed the curtains to shut out the cold and darkness. In another house the blinds were closed tightly. But Scrooge could see the shadows of people inside, dancing and laughing.
Then several lovely teenage girls came out of a house, wearing fur boots and warm, hooded coats. Chattering happily, they hurried next door to invite their neighbor to join their family for dinner.
Scrooge listened as the man accepted their invitation. "His face is glowing with joy," Scrooge thought.
He was just about to point out the man to the spirit when a church bell rang. To Scrooge's surprise, the Ghost of Christmas Present disappeared. So did everything else around him.

Scrooge heard a sound and turned to see a different phantom moving toward him. It was tall and covered in a black garment with a hood. Scrooge couldn't see its face, its body, or anything else except one thin, outstretched hand. Its mysterious presence filled Scrooge with a terrible dread.
"Am I . . . Are you the Ghost of Christmas Future?" Scrooge asked in a shaky voice.
The spirit said nothing. It only lifted its hand, pointing a finger past Scrooge.
"You're about to show me the shadows of things that will happen in the future," Scrooge said. "Is that true, spirit?"
The spirit tilted its head but still said nothing.
By now Scrooge was almost accustomed to his ghostly visitors. Even so, he felt so afraid of this new spirit that his whole body trembled.
"Ghost of the Future!" he cried. "I'm more afraid of you than the other ghosts. But I know your purpose is to do me good. I am prepared to follow where you will lead. But why won't you speak to me?"
The finger pointed again. Then the mysterious spirit began drifting in that same direction, and Scrooge followed it wearily.

As Scrooge followed the strange ghost, the darkness of its cloak seemed to expand and swallow him up. He blinked and saw they were on a bustling city street. It was daytime, and several businessmen were gathered here and there, talking.
The spirit stopped beside three men.
"Did you hear?" a stout man was saying. "The devil has welcomed back one of its own."
"Yes, I heard. I don't know how it happened, though," a very tall man said. "I only know he's dead. When did he die?"
"Last night, I believe." The third man checked his gold watch. "What was the matter with him anyway? I thought he'd never die."
"Who knows." The tall man yawned. "More importantly, what has he done with his money?"
The man with the gold watch chuckled. "He didn't leave it to any of us, that's for sure!"
"Well, it's going to be a very cheap and small funeral," the tall man said. "Should we go, just so at least a few people show up?"
The stout man looked interested. "I'd go if a nice lunch is provided."

"I know these men," Scrooge said to the ghost. "They're well known around the city. But why do you want me to hear them? Who are they discussing? It can't be Jacob Marley, because his death happened in the past. You're supposed to be showing me the future."

Suddenly the street disappeared. Scrooge was now walking through an unfamiliar part of the city with small, shabby houses. The streets were narrow and dirty, and the people looked tired and thin. Rats darted here and there, bold and bright eyed. Even the snow seemed different, with soot and dust settling upon it as soon as it touched the ground.
The spirit led Scrooge to a grubby shop where iron, rags, bottles, and other items were bought and sold. A gray-haired shopkeeper sat among the goods, smoking a pipe.

A woman entered the shop carrying a large bundle. Moments later a second woman came in with a bundle of her own. They were soon followed by a man in a faded black coat. When all three seemed startled to see the others, the shopkeeper laughed.

"You look surprised to see one another," he said. "But I heard your employer died, and so I'm not surprised to see any of you. I'll let the housekeeper show me what she has brought first. The laundrywoman can go second. The undertaker's assistant will be third."
The housekeeper dropped her bundle on the shop floor. Her expression was guilty and defiant. "Every person has a right to take care of themselves. Though I never met him, I know he always did."
"That's true, indeed!" the laundrywoman said. "He was always thinking about himself!"
The housekeeper kicked open her bundle. Inside were a couple of blankets and a set of bed curtains. "A dead man will not miss these things."
"He won't miss these either," the laundrywoman said, opening her own bundle. It contained men's clothing, a few silver teaspoons, and a worn pair of boots.

"His things didn't help him in the end," the undertaker's assistant said. "They could not have comforted him while he lay gasping out his last breath, all by himself." The man opened the bundle. It held only a pencil case, some buttons, and a few other small things.
Scrooge watched in horror as the shopkeeper examined everything before him. "These servants stole from their employer!" Scrooge cried. "They have no respect for him, even when he's dead!"
As usual, the spirit didn't answer.
Scrooge sighed in frustration. Then he suddenly realized why the ghost was showing him these scenes.
"Oh!" he said. "You're telling me, spirit, that the situation of this unfortunate man could be my situation too. You want me to know that I must change or I will share his fate. Is that correct?"
The spirit lifted its finger, and the grubby shop disappeared. Now the two of them were standing in Scrooge's bedroom. A familiar form lay on the bed, not moving or even breathing.
"Oh!" Scrooge gazed in horror at the lifeless body on the bed. "The dead man whom everyone is discussing—it's me!"
The spirit nodded slowly.
"I promise, I have learned my lesson!" Scrooge said. "But surely there must be at least one person who will feel strong emotions about my death. If so, please show that person to me."
Once again Scrooge felt himself swallowed up in the darkness of the spirit's cloak. He emerged a moment later into daylight, in a room occupied by a young mother and a few children.
The mother paced the room, stopping now and then to peer out the window. Finally the door opened and a young man came in, stomping the snow off his boots.
"Is it good news or bad?" the woman asked anxiously.
"I think it's mostly bad news," the man said. "We still don't have enough money to pay off our whole debt."
"Oh, no." She collapsed into a chair.
"Wait! There is still hope, Caroline," her husband said. "I just learned something—he is dead."
The woman gasped. "He's dead? But that means our debt will be transferred to someone else. Who will we owe money to now?"

"I don't know," her husband said. "But at least we have more time to gather the money we owe. And I doubt anyone could be as heartless as Ebenezer Scrooge was. So, perhaps we can sleep tonight with lighter hearts."
Scrooge scowled. "This isn't fair, spirit! I barely know these people. Show me someone whose opinion I know better—and respect."

As usual, the ghost said nothing. It only flung its cloak wide, sweeping away the room and returning Scrooge to the busy streets of London. Then it pointed its bony hand at two well-dressed gentlemen talking on a busy corner.

"I know those two men very well," Scrooge said with a nod. "Like the others we saw earlier, they're wealthy and important businessmen. And I always made a point of treating them fairly in business. I'm sure they respect me a great deal for that."
Scrooge moved closer to his acquaintances.
"How are you?" one businessman said to the other.
"I'm very well, and how are you?" the second man said. "Did you hear that old Ebenezer Scrooge has died?"
"Yes, I heard something about that." The first man wrapped his scarf more tightly around his neck. "Brr. It's quite cold today, isn't it?"
"The weather is right for Christmastime, though, I suppose," the second man said. "Do you like to ice skate?"
"No." The first man chuckled. "My oldest son enjoys it, though. He'll be so happy about this weather. Good morning!"
With a tip of their hats, the two men parted ways.

Scrooge glared after them as they disappeared. "We did so much business together, and that's all they have to say about my death? Why, the cold weather was more interesting to them than the news of my passing."
The spirit didn't move.
"Show me something else, spirit!" Scrooge demanded angrily. "This time I want to see some truly sad feelings about death."
Whoosh! The ghost swept his black cloak, gathering Scrooge into darkness. When Scrooge could see again, he found himself back in Bob Cratchit's house.
"That's more like it," Scrooge said. "My clerk and his family will be very sad to learn of my passing. If nothing else, it means his paycheck will stop until he finds other employment."

The Cratchit home was much quieter than the last time Scrooge had seen it. Bob Cratchit was nowhere to be seen, and neither was his daughter Martha. Mrs. Cratchit and Belinda were sewing by the light of the fire. Sam and Sarah were listening to Peter, who was reading quietly from the family's bible.
"'And He took a child, and set him in the midst of them,'" Peter read.
Mrs. Cratchit looked up and set her sewing down on a table. "Oh, please don't read any more, Peter. Especially not when your father gets home. It will only make poor Papa even sadder."
"There, you see?" Scrooge smiled. "The whole family is upset that I'm dead!"
The spirit stared at Scrooge for a moment before pointing back to the family.
Scrooge watched Belinda jump to her feet and hug her mother. "Oh, Mother. We all miss him terribly. What will we do?"
The other children ran over to throw their arms around the two of them.
"It's not right, Mother," Sarah said with a sob. "Why did he have to die? Why did we have to lose our precious brother?"
Scrooge gasped. The spirit was indeed showing him sadness about death. But the Cratchit family wasn't sad about Scrooge's death. They were mourning their beloved son and brother, Tiny Tim!

Scrooge was still trying to recover from his shock about Tiny Tim when Bob Cratchit arrived home. The man's cheeks were red from the cold, and he was huddled into a thick scarf. Belinda rushed to bring her father a hot cup of tea. Peter hung up Bob's coat while the younger two children folded the scarf and put it away.
Once their father was settled by the fire, Sam and Sarah hugged his knees.
"Don't be sad, Father," Sam said softly. "Tiny Tim would want us to be happy."

Bob smiled at them, though his eyes were mournful. "I know Tiny Tim would want us to be cheerful. But it's difficult to feel happy when we miss him so much, isn't it?" His gaze wandered toward the tiny crutch that was leaning against the wall. "We'll go to church tomorrow for his funeral. After that, we'll just have to try to go on with life and be happy, as best as we can."
His wife patted his hand. "Yes, we'll manage somehow."
"Oh!" Cratchit sat up a little straighter. "I meant to tell you, dear, I met Mr. Scrooge's nephew, Fred, in the street today."
"Did you?" His wife brushed a few tears from her eyes.
"Yes. Fred remembered me and greeted me by name," Cratchit said. "I was quite impressed by his friendliness because we only met a few times. He even noticed that I looked unusually sad."
"So unlike his uncle," Mrs. Cratchit murmured.

Her husband nodded. "That's for sure. I told Fred the sad news about our Tim. He said, 'I am heartily sorry for it, Mr. Cratchit, and heartily sorry for your good wife. If I can be of help to you in any way, please come to me.' And then he gave me his card." Cratchit smiled weakly. "It truly seemed as if Fred had known Tiny Tim and missed him."
Mrs. Cratchit looked down. "Nobody who knew Tiny Tim will ever forget him," she said softly.
"No, never, Mother!" the children cried.
"We must also remember how patient and mild Tim was," Cratchit said. "His example will remind us never to be unkind to others. Tiny Tim wouldn't like it."
"No, never, Father!" the children said.

Scrooge felt tears suddenly welling up in his eyes. He never could have imagined that so many people would feel such strong love for a young child. Then Scrooge remembered his sister, Fan, and the happy times they'd spent together as children. Fan had meant so much to him back then.

Whoosh! The phantom startled him by waving its cloak over the whole scene. Now the Cratchits were standing together in a snowy churchyard. Martha was there, too, holding her mother's hand. Friends and neighbors stood nearby, and Fred was hurrying to join everyone.
"I'm so sorry for your loss, Mr. and Mrs. Cratchit," Fred said, taking off his hat.
"Thank you, sir," Bob Cratchit said, shaking Fred's hand. "We already miss Tiny Tim very much."
"He was a wonderful boy," Fred said.
Cratchit's eyes filled with tears. "He was indeed."
Scrooge watched Tiny Tim's brothers and sisters move closer to Tiny Tim's grave, all holding hands.
"I wish Tiny Tim could have lived another week, at least," Peter said. "He always loved Christmas. It doesn't seem fair that he has to miss it."
"It doesn't seem fair at all!" Scrooge said. "I've seen enough, spirit. I've learned my lesson. Please take me home."
The spirit didn't speak. But from the way it lifted its arm, Scrooge knew what it was telling him: "Not yet. There is more to see."
Tiny Tim's funeral was gone, and now Scrooge was back in the heart of the bustling city. He looked around at the shops lining both sides of the street.
"Why have you brought me here?" he asked the spirit. "It's not a place where I ever spent time."
The spirit drifted toward a particular shop. Scrooge followed, squinting to make out the name on the sign out front. It was dusted with fresh snow.

"Richard Wilkins, Tailor," he read aloud. "Oh! We're back to visit Dick Wilkins again. But I'm still quite confused, spirit. Are you saying that Wilkins is the only one who will miss me after I've died?"
The spirit stared at Scrooge for a moment before beckoning him to follow. Together they entered the tailor's shop.
Inside the shop Scrooge could see that Wilkins' face had more wrinkles now. But Wilkins' smile looked brighter than ever as he spoke to a young boy.
"Tell me, Edward," Wilkins said. "Have you been outside, looking at all the Christmas decorations in the neighborhood?"

"Yes, Grandfather," the boy said eagerly. "I love all of them—especially the wreaths and garlands. It's sunny out, but guess what! It's so cold that the lake in the park is frozen. I heard people saying they've never seen such a perfect day for ice skating."
"Hmm." Wilkins chuckled. "It sounds like someone might like to go skating today. Maybe I can close the shop early, and we can go before dinner. How does that sound?"
"Really?" Edward said. "We can go skating?"
"Of course," Wilkins said. "When I opened this shop, I promised myself that I would never let work become more important than family. And do you know who taught me this valuable lesson?"
"Who, Grandfather?" Edward asked.
"A very wealthy businessman named Ebenezer Scrooge," Wilkins said. "He actually taught me many important things about work."
Scrooge gasped. "This is wonderful, spirit! Good old Dick Wilkins sounds as if he is quite fond of me. He always did look up to me when we worked together."
Wilkins reached for a newspaper that was lying on the table. He opened it to a page with obituaries.

"See this notice, Edward? Mr. Scrooge died recently. But he was survived by no family, except for one nephew. And from what I hear, he had no friends at all." Wilkins shook his head. "It's a shame. I knew him long ago, and he was a nice enough fellow back then."
"Were the two of you once friends then?" Edward asked curiously.
"Well, I tried my best to be his friend." Wilkins folded the newspaper, setting it aside.

"We worked together for a year or two. After that, he started a new business with a clever businessman named Marley. At the time Ebenezer was courting a lovely young woman named Belle who seemed to make him happy. But with every passing month, Ebenezer spent more time working and less time doing anything else. I went to visit him a few times, but he had no time for me or anyone else. He was too busy thinking about money." Wilkins shook his head. "Remember this, Edward: A relationship that's neglected will wither and die."
Wilkins suddenly stood up. "But never mind all that; it's ancient history now. I'll finish up a couple of things at the shop, and then we can go skating."

Before Scrooge could say anything, the scene faded, and was quickly replaced by another. He and the ghost now stood in a warm sitting room. Flower petals were strewn on the floor, and white fabric was draped over furniture. Belle was there, her hair now touched with gray. She was beaming at a beautiful young woman wearing a wedding dress.
Belle adjusted one of the sleeves on the young woman's dress. "There, that looks perfect. I can hardly believe it—my youngest child is getting married!"
Her daughter hugged her. "I'm excited but also very nervous."
"I understand." Belle smiled. "I was nervous too. But just remember how happy your father has made me all these years. I can't imagine my life without him."
"You were older than I am when you married him," the daughter said. "Other men must have courted you before you met Papa."
Belle shrugged. "I suppose they did." She tilted her head with a thoughtful expression. "In fact, I nearly got married once before."
"What?" Her daughter looked shocked. "Why, I never knew that! Who was the man you almost married?"
"His name was Ebenezer Scrooge," Belle said. "I loved him, but I realized in the nick of time that he loved something else more."
"Oh!" The daughter peered closely at Belle. "He fell in love with another woman?"
Belle laughed. "No, he fell in love with money, and only that. And then, thank goodness, I later met my true love, your papa."
Scrooge felt a sharp jolt at Belle's words. Then Dick Wilkins' words floated through his mind too: "A relationship that is neglected will wither and die."
Scrooge clutched his head in pain. "What have I done to myself?" he thought. He knew the answer. He had allowed the most precious things in his life to wither and die.

The ghost lifted its arm once again. Scrooge saw that they were back in the churchyard where Tiny Tim's funeral had taken place. Snow lay on the ground as before, but there was no clear, bright sky. Instead gray clouds dimmed the weak rays of the sun. The same priest stood in front of a different grave, looking down at a plain wooden coffin. This time no mourners were looking on. Only a couple of large men, gravediggers with spades, stood nearby.

A cruel, cold wind howled, making the bare tree branches shudder and creak. The priest shivered too, pulling his robe closer for warmth. A moment later he took out his pocket watch and checked the time.
He nodded at the gravediggers. "Nobody is coming to this poor soul's burial. Go ahead and fill in the grave."
As the priest hurried back into the church, the men set to work. They filled in the hole as quickly as they could. Then one jammed a square stone into place at the head of the grave.
Scrooge stepped forward to see it. But he already knew what name he would see carved into the tombstone: Ebenezer Scrooge.
"Nobody came to my funeral," he whispered. "Not Fred and his family, nor any of my business acquaintances. Even the priest didn't stay for the whole thing."

The spirit lifted its arm, and for a moment, Scrooge was in a different place. It was a bedroom in Fred's house. Fred's youngest daughter was lying there, pale and ill. Fred's wife was kneeling beside her. Then Fred himself hurried in with a damp cloth, which he used to tenderly wipe the girl's face.
"It's nearly time for your uncle's funeral," Fred's wife said. "You said you wanted to go."
"I did." Fred adjusted his daughter's blankets. "But that was before our girl became ill."
"She's getting better, and the church isn't far," his wife said. "It wouldn't take you very long to pay your respects."
"Yes, Papa," the young girl herself said, her voice rough with illness. "I'm all right. Please go."
Fred shrugged. "I haven't spoken to Uncle Scrooge in months. He didn't seek my company when he was alive. So, I don't expect he'll miss me now that he's dead."
Scrooge swallowed hard. "I see," he thought. "I see."

With that, Fred's house disappeared, and the phantom pointed its finger upward at the sky. Scrooge looked up and watched the sun sink rapidly toward the horizon, moving as quickly as a racing horse. Just as quickly, it rose in the east. It flew across the sky, and then set again. It rose and set, over and over, moving faster and faster. Days, weeks, and months passed in a matter of minutes.

Finally the ghost turned its finger once again in the direction of Scrooge's lonely grave. The grave looked even lonelier now. It was late summer, and grass had grown in over the bare earth. Then weeds had sprouted, twisting vines and brambles, grabbing at the headstone and hiding the name on it. Someone had discarded a rusty tin can there, along with several scraps of newspaper. While nearby graves had flowers or mementos laid upon them, nobody had left anything to honor Ebenezer Scrooge.
Scrooge stared at the headstone, his face pale and thoughtful. "Answer me one question, spirit. Are these the shadows of things that will happen, or are they just shadows of things that may happen?"
The phantom didn't answer. It only continued pointing at the grave.
"But, spirit, I'm not the man I was!" Scrooge cried. "I won't be the same man after what I've seen tonight. Why would you show me this terrible scene if I'm past all hope?"
The spirit pointed from the grave to Scrooge, and then back again.
Scrooge fell onto the ground. "Good spirit. Please tell me that it's still possible to change my future by changing my life in the present. That is all I want to know."
The pointing hand trembled.
"I promise to honor Christmas in my heart," Scrooge said. "I'll try to remember its lessons all year long. Please tell me there is time, and I can still make things better!"
In desperation, Scrooge grabbed the spirit's hand. The Ghost of Christmas Future yanked free. A moment later the ghost shrunk and collapsed until it was nothing but a wooden bedpost.
Scrooge gasped and sat up. The wooden bedpost was on his own bed—he was back in his bedroom!
He leaped out of bed, eager to make amends for his past behavior.
"Oh, Jacob Marley, thank you for this precious lesson!" he thought. "I am still here and alive, which means I still have time to change my future. I know I can do it!"

Scrooge was so overwhelmed by all his new emotions that he could barely dress himself. He turned his garments inside out, and then started to put them on upside down. He even tore a hole in one of his best socks.

"I don't know what to do!" he said, laughing and crying at the same time. "I feel as light as a feather. I am as happy as an angel and as merry as a schoolboy. A merry Christmas to everybody! A happy new year to everyone in the world!"
He ran into his sitting room and looked around at the familiar surroundings. Instead of seeing the dull apartment of a selfish man, he now saw only wonder and beauty.

"There's the lovely cup that held my tea!" he said, dancing around the room. "There are the door and chair that the ghost of Jacob Marley used. Oh, and there's the spot where that giant, the Ghost of Christmas Present, sat! It's all true. It all really happened."
He laughed loudly, the first genuine laugh he'd let out in many years.

"I don't know what day of the month it is," Scrooge thought. "I don't know how long I was among the three spirits. I don't know anything, so I am like a newborn baby. And I'd much rather be this innocent baby than the awful man I was before."

Just then he heard the church bells ring out the hour. He ran to the window and yanked it open so he could hear the glorious bells more clearly. Sticking his head outside, he saw that the morning was bright and clear. Sunlight washed everything below in a beautiful golden glow.
Then Scrooge spotted a boy, dressed in his best clothes.
"You there!" Scrooge called. "Tell me, what's today?"
The boy looked up with a confused expression. "Pardon me, sir?"
"What day is it, my fine fellow?" Scrooge asked. "Tell me the date!"
"Why, it's Christmas Day, of course," the boy said.

"Christmas Day!" Scrooge said, now speaking to himself rather than the boy. "So, I haven't missed it. The spirits did all their work in one short night!" Noticing the boy giving him an odd look, Scrooge added, "I'd like to request a favor. Do you know the meat shop around the corner, the one with the large turkey hanging in the window?"
"Yes, I know that shop," the boy said.
"What an intelligent boy!" Scrooge said. "A remarkable boy! Do you know whether they've sold that fine bird yet? Not the smaller ones—I'm only interested in the big one."
"I just passed by and it's hanging there now," the boy said.

"Wonderful!" Scrooge beamed with delight. "Go and fetch the owner of the shop and bring him here. Tell him I want to buy that turkey. When he arrives, I'll pay him and instruct him where he should deliver it."
The boy still looked confused.
"Come back with the man," Scrooge said, "and I'll give you a few coins. Come back with him in less than five minutes and I'll give you even more money!"
Swiftly understanding that offer, the boy took off like a shot.

Scrooge watched him go, smiling with pleasure. "I'll send the turkey to Bob Cratchit's house, and the family won't know who sent it." He rubbed his hands together gleefully. "They'll never be able to eat it all. Why, it's twice the size of Tiny Tim!"
Soon the shopkeeper arrived. He was out of breath and looked as confused as the boy had looked at first.

Scrooge was all smiles when he paid the boy for his errand. He chuckled out loud when he paid the man for the turkey. And he laughed even more joyfully when he gave extra money to the shop owner. That was to pay for the cab that would transport the large bird across town.
With these tasks accomplished, Scrooge changed into his best clothes. Then he set out into the London streets. For the first time since childhood, he was about to enjoy Christmas.
Outside, Scrooge walked along, greeting everyone on the streets with a delighted smile.
A pair of men noticed his joy and smiled in return.
"Good morning, sir!" one said, tipping his hat. "Merry Christmas to you."
"Thank you, sir, and I wish you the same," Scrooge said.

He hadn't gone much farther when he spotted one of the gentlemen who had visited his office the day before. It sent a pang through his heart now. Scrooge had sent him away, yelling horribly about putting poor people in prison.
"My dear sir!" Scrooge hurried to catch up to the gentleman. "A merry Christmas to you!"
"Mr. Scrooge?" the gentleman said in surprise.
"That's my name," Scrooge said. "Though I fear you may not think much of it. Still, I hope a generous donation to the poor will change your mind." He whispered an amount of money into the man's ear.
The man's eyes went wide. "Mr. Scrooge, are you serious? You want to donate all that money?"
"I am serious," Scrooge said. "Not a penny less. Will you please do me the favor of accepting it, and seeing that it helps the poor?"
"I will, of course! Thank you!"
Scrooge nodded. "Come to see me at my office tomorrow. I'll give you the money then."
Scrooge continued on his way, patting children on the head and giving coins to beggars.
"What a wonderful, beautiful holiday!" he thought.
Finally he reached his nephew's house. He wanted to stop and knock but his knees trembled. He had to pass by the door a dozen times before he finally found the courage to knock.
A servant brought him to the dining room. Scrooge peered nervously into the room filled with Fred and his family, as well as some guests.
"Why, bless my soul! Who's that?" Fred said.
"I've . . . I've . . ." Scrooge's voice quaked. "I've, um, come to dinner. Will you let me in, Fred?"
"Of course!" Fred took his uncle's hand and nearly shook Scrooge's arm off.

The family immediately made Scrooge feel at home. He was welcomed by Fred's wife and by their children. Other guests chatted politely with him. It was a wonderful party, with delicious food and entertaining games. Scrooge stayed late and enjoyed himself thoroughly.
Even so, he was up early the next morning to go to work. In fact, he arrived even earlier than usual.
"Good," he thought as he sat at his desk. "Cratchit isn't here yet. I hope he comes in late this morning."
And so he did. Cratchit was a full 18 minutes late when he finally arrived. He rushed in, leaping onto his stool as if he were trying to catch up with the clock.
"What do you mean by showing up here at this time of day?" Scrooge growled.
"I'm sorry, sir," Cratchit said meekly. "I . . . My family and I . . ."
"Step this way!"
Cratchit cowered as he followed his boss across the room. "It's only once a year, sir. It won't happen again."

"Well, the current way of doing things around here is unacceptable," Scrooge snapped. "And therefore . . ." He couldn't stop a smile from taking the place of his angry scowl. "I'm going to raise your salary! Merry Christmas, Bob!"
Cratchit gazed at him in amazement. "Are you serious, Mr. Scrooge?"

Scrooge clapped him on the back. "I haven't given you a very merry Christmas for many years now. But I wish to make up for that. I'll raise your salary, and do whatever I can to help your family. That includes hiring the best doctors for Tiny Tim."
"But . . . But . . ." Tears filled Cratchit's eyes. "Thank you, sir."
"Don't thank me, Bob. Please go home to your family and take another day off!"

Scrooge was as good as his word. Thanks to the doctors he hired, the tragic scene shown by the Ghost of Christmas Future never appeared. Instead Tiny Tim thrived. Not only that, but he also grew up thinking of Ebenezer Scrooge as a second father.

And Scrooge didn't stop there, with the Cratchit family. Instead he became a charitable man. Everyone who knew him observed the same thing. He kept the kind and loving spirit of Christmas with him all year long.
"That's what I strive for every day of my life," he said to anyone who asked him about it. "May that be said of all of us—that we are kind and loving. As Tiny Tim might say, God bless us, everyone!"
